q: 1. For given workability the grading requiring the least amount of water is one that gives
options: greatest surface area for the given cement and aggregates
least surface area for the given cement and aggregates
lest weight for the given cement and aggregates
greatest weight for the given cement and aggregates
explain: A grading that produces the least surface area of aggregate particles (for a given volume) requires the least amount of water to wet and coat the surfaces, achieving the desired workability with minimum water.

q: 2. For constant w/c ratio if the aggregate/cement ratio is reduced, the workability of concrete
explain: Reducing the aggregate-cement ratio (i.e., using relatively more cement paste) while keeping water-cement ratio constant provides more paste to lubricate the aggregates, increasing workability.

q: 3. Slump test is done for
explain: The slump test is a standard method specifically used to assess the consistency and workability of fresh concrete.

q: 4. Vacat's apparatus is used to test the following property of concrete
explain: The Vicat apparatus is used to determine the standard consistency of cement paste, which is a fundamental property tested before other cement tests are conducted.

q: 5. The minimum water-cement ratio to obtain workable concrete is
explain: A minimum water-cement ratio of about 0.40 is generally needed to produce a concrete mix with sufficient workability for proper placement and compaction.

q: 6. The slump test of concrete is used to measure its
explain: The slump test is primarily used to assess the consistency of fresh concrete, which is an indicator of its water content and workability.

q: 7. If slump of concrete mix 70 mm, its workability is considered to be
explain: A slump value of 70 mm typically falls within the medium workability range as per standard slump classification.

q: 8. Internal friction between the ingredients of concrete, is decreased by using
explain: Using more water (which lubricates the mix) along with coarse aggregate (which has less surface area/friction compared to fine material) reduces the internal friction between the concrete ingredients.

q: 9. A compaction factor of 0.88 indicates that the workability of concrete mix is
explain: A compaction factor of 0.88 corresponds to the medium workability range as per the IS classification table.

q: 10. More water should not be added in the concrete mix so as to increase
explain: Adding extra water beyond the design mix raises the water-cement ratio, which in turn reduces strength and durability — so all of these are adversely affected.

q: 11. Workability of concrete may be improved by adding
explain: All these admixtures/materials - fly ash, hydrated lime, calcium chloride, and bentonite - are known to improve the workability of concrete mixes when added in appropriate quantities.

q: 12. Workability of concrete may be improved by adding
explain: Air-entraining agents, foaming agents, oily agents, and aluminium compounds are all known types of admixtures that can improve the workability of concrete when properly used.

q: 13. Workability of concrete is directly proportional to
explain: Better grading of the aggregate (proper distribution of particle sizes) results in reduced voids and less water demand, which directly improves and is proportional to workability.

q: 14. Workability of concrete is inversely proportional to
explain: As the time of transit increases, some water evaporates and initial hydration begins, causing the mix to stiffen - hence workability decreases (inversely proportional) with increasing transit time.

q: 15. The shrinkage of concrete
options: is proportional to water content in the mix
explain: Shrinkage of concrete is influenced by water content, cement content, and generally increases (though at a decreasing rate) with the age of concrete - all these factors together describe shrinkage behaviour.

q: 16. If 50 kg of fine aggregates and 100 kg of coarse aggregates are mixed in a concrete whose water cement ratio is 0.6, the weight of water required for harsh mix is
explain: For a harsh mix using this water-cement ratio, calculations based on the given cement quantity used in the book's worked example give a water requirement of about 14 kg.

q: 17. The nature of fresh concrete is
explain: Freshly mixed (unset) concrete behaves as a plastic material - it can be moulded, placed, and compacted into any shape before it hardens.

q: 18. Too wet concrete may cause
explain: Excessively wet concrete leads to multiple defects together - reduced strength, laitance formation, segregation of ingredients, and lower final density.

q: 19. For batching 1:3:6 and water cement ratio 0.6 both by weight, the quantity of water required per bag, is
explain: For a 50 kg cement bag with a water-cement ratio of 0.6 by weight, the water required = 0.6 x 50 = 30 kg.

q: 20. Internal friction between the ingredients of concrete is decreased by using
explain: Using more water (lubrication) along with coarser aggregate (lower surface area) reduces internal friction between the mix ingredients.

q: 21. Water required per bag of cement is
explain: As a general rule referenced in this text, about 28 kg (litres) of water is required per 50 kg bag of cement for a typical nominal mix.

q: 22. CRRI charts are used to obtain relationship between strength of concrete and
explain: CRRI (Central Road Research Institute) charts are specifically used to establish the relationship between concrete strength and water-cement ratio for mix design purposes.

q: 23. Higher workability of concrete is required if the structure is
explain: Thin sections with heavy/congested reinforcement require a highly workable mix so that concrete can flow properly around closely spaced bars and fully compact.

q: 24. Workability of concrete is inversely proportional to
explain: As transit/transport time increases, the concrete progressively loses slump and workability due to early hydration and moisture loss, making workability inversely related to transit time.

q: 25. Strength of concrete increases with
explain: Finer cement particles have greater surface area available for hydration, which speeds up and enhances early strength development, hence increasing concrete strength.

q: 26. Pick up the correct statement form the following:
options: higher workability indicates unexpected increase in the moisture content
higher workability indicates deficiency of sand
if the concrete mix is dry, the slump is zero
concrete mix having zero slump is unsuitable for high strength
explain: All the listed statements are individually true observations relating slump/workability to moisture, sand content and mix dryness, so 'all of the above' is correct.

q: 27. Increase in moisture content in concrete
explain: Excess moisture content in concrete effectively raises the water-cement ratio in the system, which reduces the resulting compressive strength.

q: 28. Workability of concrete mix with low water cement ratio is determined by
explain: For stiff, low water-cement ratio mixes where the slump test is unreliable (zero or near-zero slump), the compaction factor test is the preferred method to assess workability.

q: 29. Pick up the correct statement from the following:
options: the free water is the amount of water added while mixing and the amount of water held on the surface of the aggregates prior to mixing
the total water is the free water and the amount actually absorbed by the aggregates
explain: Free water and total water are defined the opposite way to how they are stated here — free water excludes surface moisture already on the aggregate before mixing, so neither statement is technically correct as worded.

q: 30. The risk of segregation is more for
explain: Wetter mixes, a larger proportion of maximum-size aggregate, and coarser grading all reduce cohesion of the mix, increasing the likelihood that coarse aggregate separates from the mortar (segregation).

q: 31. For preparing ordinary concrete, the quantity of water used is
options: 5% by weight of aggregate plus 20 % by weight of cement
10% by weight of aggregate plus 10 % by weight of cement
5% by weight of aggregate plus 30 % by weight of cement
30% by weight of aggregate plus 10 % by weight of cement
explain: As per the nominal mix water guideline in this text, ordinary concrete water content is taken as 5% by weight of aggregate plus 30% by weight of cement.

q: 32. To hydrate 500 kg cement fully, water needed is
explain: Using the theoretical water requirement of about 0.25-0.26 (times cement mass) for full hydration, 500 kg of cement requires approximately 130 kg of water, as per this text.

q: 33. The maximum water cement ratio in plain concrete to ensure durability in mild exposure is limited to
explain: For plain concrete under mild exposure conditions, the maximum permissible water-cement ratio specified for durability is 0.7.

q: 34. For a given degree of hydration, the effect of increasing water cement ratio in concrete
explain: A higher water-cement ratio results in a more porous cement paste structure with larger and more interconnected capillary pores, thereby increasing the permeability of concrete.

q: 35. For a given water cement ratio, with passage of time, the permeability
explain: As hydration continues over time, the cement gel progressively fills the capillary pore structure, which decreases the permeability of concrete for a given water-cement ratio.

q: 36. The water cement ratio for ferrocement mix should be
explain: A relatively low water-cement ratio of 0.35 to 0.40 is recommended for ferrocement mixes so that the rich mortar can properly penetrate the closely spaced mesh while maintaining strength.

q: 37. If water cement ratio is more,
options: the durability of the concrete will be more
the durability of the concrete will be less
the durability of the concrete will not be affected
explain: A higher water-cement ratio increases the porosity and permeability of hardened concrete, which reduces its durability against attack by external agents.

q: 38. Low water-cement ratio in concrete:
options: improves the frost resistance of concrete
explain: A low water-cement ratio produces a denser paste, which simultaneously lowers permeability, raises compressive strength, and improves resistance to frost/freeze-thaw damage.

q: 39. Steel mould used for slump test is in the form of :
explain: The standard slump test mould is a frustum of a cone (Abrams cone), which is filled with concrete and lifted vertically to measure the resulting slump.

q: 40. The durability of concrete is proportion to :
explain: Durability of concrete is closely linked to the cement-aggregate ratio, since it governs the density and impermeability of the paste matrix surrounding the aggregate.

q: 41. The strength of concrete increase with decreases in :
explain: Strength of concrete is inversely related to the water-cement ratio — as the water-cement ratio decreases, the paste becomes denser and strength increases (Abrams' law).

q: 42. The steel mould used for slump test is in the form of :
explain: As with the standard slump test mould, it is shaped as a frustum of a cone (Abrams cone) open at both ends.
